title: Quiz: External Data - Intermediary
prompt: Test your knowledge of memory sections (.data, .bss, .text), ASCII string literals, pointers, and handling command-line arguments in assembly.

questions.question: What exactly does the `adrp` instruction do to calculate a memory address?
options: Shifts a 21-bit immediate right by 12 bits and adds it to the Stack Pointer.
Shifts a signed 21-bit immediate left by 12 bits and adds it to the PC with the bottom 12 bits cleared to zero.
Adds a 64-bit immediate directly to the Frame Pointer.
Multiplies the immediate by 4096 and adds it to the Link Register.
questions.explanation: ADRP shifts a signed, 21-bit immediate left by 12 bits, adds it to the value of PC with the bottom 12 bits cleared to zero, and writes the result to a register.
questions.hint: ADRP stands for Address of Page, which is why it forces a 4KB aligned memory region by manipulating the bottom 12 bits.

questions.question: Why does it not make sense to initialize memory to non-zero values (using `.word` or `.hword`) within the `.bss` section?
options: Because the .bss section is strictly read-only memory.
Because all .bss memory is zeroed before program execution by the OS.
Because the assembler will throw a syntax error during compilation.
Because .bss is reserved exclusively for string literals.
questions.explanation: All bss memory is zeroed before program execution, so initializing memory to non-zero values there doesn't make sense.
questions.hint: The OS wipes this entire section clean when the program is loaded into RAM.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the `.ascii` and `.string` pseudo-ops?
options: .string automatically adds a null-terminator byte at the end of the character array, while .ascii does not.
.ascii is for read-only memory, while .string is for read/write memory.
.string stores characters as 16-bit unicode, while .ascii uses 7-bit characters.
There is no difference; they are exact aliases.
questions.explanation: In C, strings are null terminated, which could be done manually using .ascii and a .byte 0, but is done more conveniently with .asciz or .string.
questions.hint: C requires a specific byte at the end of an array to know where a string stops.

questions.question: In the typical memory layout shown in the lecture, which section immediately follows the `.data` section moving towards higher memory?
options: .text
OS
.bss
Stack
questions.explanation: The sections are located in low memory, just after the section reserved for the OS kernel, in the order of: .text, .data, and then .bss.
questions.hint: Look at how the zero-initialized data sits below the programmer-initialized data.

questions.question: What happens if you declare a static variable in C without explicitly initializing it (e.g., `static int count;`)?
options: It contains garbage data from the stack.
It is initialized implicitly to 0.
It causes a compile-time error.
It is stored in the .text section.
questions.explanation: Static variables are initialized implicitly to 0, unlike stack variables which are not implicitly initialized.
questions.hint: Because they are stored in the .bss section if uninitialized, the OS handles their starting value.
